drills.q: What does saying an algorithm is O(n log n) tell you?
options: How its cost grows as the input grows, and nothing about how long it takes today
That it is faster than any quadratic algorithm
Its running time in seconds, up to a machine-dependent constant
That it is optimal for comparison-based problems
drills.why: A quadratic algorithm with a small constant beats a linearithmic one with a large one, for every input below the crossover. Asymptotic analysis says where an algorithm goes; measurement says where it is.

drills.q: Why does every serious sorting library include insertion sort?
options: It is quadratic and it is faster below some threshold
It is stable and merge sort is not
It needs no extra memory for small arrays
It handles already-sorted input in linear time
drills.why: The threshold is somewhere between 8 and 32 elements and was chosen by measuring. Asymptotic reasoning cannot produce that number, because it is entirely about the constants the notation discards.

options: The problems whose proposed answers can be checked in polynomial time
The problems that cannot be solved in polynomial time
The problems requiring randomness to solve efficiently
The problems solvable only by exhaustive search
drills.why: Every problem in P is in NP, because solving it is one way to check it. The open question is whether the reverse holds.

drills.q: What does the "nondeterministic" in NP mean?
options: A machine allowed to guess, which is the same as an answer that is easy to check
A machine that makes random choices
A machine whose running time varies between runs
A machine with unbounded parallelism
drills.why: It is the source of most of the confusion about the class, and it does not mean random.

options: It is in NP and every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time
It has been proved to require exponential time
It has no known approximation algorithm
It is the hardest problem anyone has found by experiment
drills.why: Cook and Levin showed in 1971 that Boolean satisfiability is one, which is what made reduction into the technique that organises the whole subject.

drills.q: Which direction of reduction actually gets work done?
options: Reducing your problem to one somebody has already built a good solver for
Reducing a known hard problem to yours, to prove yours is hard
Both are equally common in practice
Neither; reductions are a theoretical device
drills.why: Scheduling, register allocation, layout, dependency resolution and verification all get translated into satisfiability and handed over. It is the option people most often fail to consider.

drills.q: Satisfiability is NP-complete, and solvers settle instances with millions of variables. Why?
options: Real instances have structure, and a solver that learns from conflicts exploits it
Modern hardware has made the exponential tolerable
The solvers are approximate and may return a wrong answer
Industrial instances are all in a polynomial subclass
drills.why: Worst-case complexity describes an adversary choosing your input. Most of the time nobody is, which is the same observation that made equivalence checking practical in unit 015.

drills.q: On the pigeonhole instances, how did brute force and propagate-and-branch compare at twenty variables?
options: 1048576 assignments against 103 decisions
1048576 assignments against about 1000 decisions
They were within a factor of two
The solver was slower, because pigeonhole is its worst case
drills.why: Measured. At 56 variables the exhaustive search is about 72 quadrillion assignments and the solver settles it in 65561. Both curves are exponential and the slopes are what differ.

drills.q: What does NP-hard tell you to do?
options: Stop looking for a fast exact general algorithm, and pick one of four other plans
Abandon the problem
Use randomisation
Prove your instances are in P
drills.why: Approximate, reduce to a solver, exploit your structure, or notice your instances are small. Giving up is the bad plan, and writing your own exact solver for a problem the world already has one for is the second bad plan.

drills.q: Greedy vertex cover adds both endpoints of an uncovered edge. What does that buy?
options: A cover never worse than twice the best, with a one-sentence proof
The exact minimum on graphs without triangles
A cover within a constant additive term of the best
Nothing provable; it is a heuristic
drills.why: The edges you picked share no vertices, so any cover needs at least one endpoint from each, and you took two.

drills.q: Subset sum with a table of size target+1 runs in time proportional to n times target. Is that polynomial?
options: No, because the target's size in bits is what counts as input length
Yes, and it proves subset sum is in P
Yes, but only for positive integers
No, because the table lookup is not constant time
drills.why: It is pseudo-polynomial, and it is nonetheless why the problem is routine whenever the numbers are small. Knowing which parameter your instance keeps small is most of escaping a hardness result.

drills.q: What lives in PSPACE that does not appear to be in NP?
options: Deciding a winning strategy in a two-player game
Boolean satisfiability
Graph colouring
Integer factorisation
drills.why: Polynomial memory and any amount of time. Several model checking questions live there too.

drills.q: What is the difference between undecidable and intractable?
options: One says no algorithm exists; the other says every algorithm is slow
They are the same for problems with infinite input domains
Intractable problems become decidable with more memory
Undecidable problems have approximation algorithms and intractable ones do not
drills.why: Confusing them is common and leads to the wrong plan in both directions.

drills.q: Two correct encodings of the same problem into satisfiability...
options: Routinely differ by orders of magnitude in solving time
Take the same time, since they describe the same problem
Differ only in the number of variables, not the time
Cannot both be correct
drills.why: A reduction is only useful if it produces instances the solver is good at. Choosing between encodings is a real skill rather than a formality.

drills.q: Why does Part IV end without mentioning caches or pipelines?
options: It is about what machines can do in principle, and that is also the limit of its usefulness
Those details do not affect asymptotic cost
They belong to hardware rather than to computer science
They are covered by the constants in the notation
drills.why: Two algorithms with identical asymptotic cost can differ by ten times on a real machine because one walks memory in a way the hardware likes. Part V is about that machine.
